newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Grain-Some rain falls as planting nears.
newsitem.headline: Australian Grain-Some rain falls as planting nears.

text.p: The biggest news in a quiet grains market last week was the first crack in Australia's long dry in its eastern wheatbelt, as some rain fell on the southern state of Victoria.
As the week ended brokers and traders began to look for a fall in Australian wheat prices, a turnaround from views a week earlier that a mid-1996-style price surge rise loomed.
No rain fell in New South Wales (NSW) to break that state's dry and the fall in Victoria was patchy and not fully in areas wheat farmers wanted.
But any rain was good news with the 1997/98 wheat planting imminent and the autumn dry one of the most severe on record.

Victoria has had its driest April since 1988, while Sydney's April was the driest in 101 years. The seven months from last October have been Victoria's driest since 1878/79 and the second driest on record.
"It will depend on how widespread this rain is and how long it takes to fall to see if we're going to get it reflected in our prices here," broker Brendan Hillary of ANZ Futures said.
Good rain could bring wheat futures prices back by A$5.00-A$8.00 a tonne, he said.
Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders sees the prospect of an even greater price fall, with signs of a top forming in Sydney and Chicago.
"It's still very much a weather market and can remain volatile and susceptible to rumours. But there's a feeling about that we may have put in the highs for the season," he said.
He believed Sydney wheat futures could come back to the mid to low A$170 a tonne region.
Over the past week, the nearby May wheat futures contract rose by A$5.00 a tonne to A$193.00, while July 1997 added A$3.00. Prices for more distant contracts slid about A$2.00.
Hillary sees the prospect of growers now attempting to lock in current prices through options.

But overall it remained that Australia would have a smaller crop this season than the 1996/97 record 23 million tonnes, Hillary said. Preliminary forecasts put the new crop at about 17 million tonnes although one broker last week said that a continued dry could reduce it to as little as 14 million tonnes.
Rain would also pressure sorghum and barley, Hillary said.
Cash barley prices have risen strongly in the past two weeks weeks by A$10.00-A$15.00 to about A$155.00 a tonne ex farm in northwest NSW on end user demand.

The New South Wales Grains Board (NSWGB) also revealed in the week it had shipped more than 600,000 tonnes of barley so far in 1996/97, with 500,000 tonnes of this malting barley and slightly more than 500,000 tonnes of the total bound for China.
This compared with average-year sales of about 150,000 tonnes to China and had boosted NSWGB's share of the China import market to about 40 percent from about 10 percent in previous years, it said.
In cash markets last week, old crop wheat trading remained thin, with prices moving with futures prices.

Good NSW sorghum yields were pressuring the market, Mitchell said, although prices remained unchanged over the past week on about A$164.00 a tonne delivered Newcastle with limited selling opportunities in nearby months and growers storing on farm.

Australian wheat shipments in the latest week amounted to 316,178 tonnes, bringing cumulative shipments to date for the October/September marketing year to 12.60 million tonnes against 8.50 million tonnes a year earlier, according to preliminary figures from the AWB on Friday.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
